issues.legal_issue: The landlord’s bona fide personal need in an eviction proceeding is ordinarily assessed as of the date the eviction petition is filed.
material_facts: The landlord sought eviction to use the building for his son’s medical practice and for his own proposed work.
The fact-finding authorities found the need bona fide when the eviction petition was filed.
The tenant relied on the son’s later entry into medical service to challenge the eviction order.
issues.conclusion: The date of filing the eviction petition was the crucial date for deciding whether the landlord’s need was bona fide; later developments did not, by themselves, change that assessment.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 21(1)(a) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, the landlord’s bona fide requirement is ordinarily assessed as of the date of the eviction application. The normal rule is that parties’ rights and obligations are determined as they stood when the litigation began, subject to cautious consideration of subsequent events that materially affect entitlement or the relief; the Court relied on Ramesh Kumar v. Kesho Ram and Kamleshwar Prasad v. Pradumanju Agarwal.

predicates.personal_need_eviction_case: A landlord brings an eviction proceeding on the ground that the premises are needed for the landlord or a family member.
predicates.need_existed_when_petition_filed: The landlord’s asserted need existed when the eviction petition was filed.

issues.definition: When a landlord seeks eviction for personal or family use and the need existed at filing, the need is assessed as of that filing.

issues.legal_issue: A subsequent development defeats an established bona fide personal need only if it completely eclipses or wholly satisfies that need.
material_facts: The landlord’s son later joined the Provincial Medical Service and was posted about 200 kilometres from the premises.
The tenant relied on the son’s employment and salary as subsequent developments undermining the need for the premises.
The fact-finding authorities had concurrently found the landlord’s need bona fide, and the later developments did not show that the need had been wholly satisfied.
issues.conclusion: The son’s later employment was insufficient to overshadow the bona fide need established at the time of the petition, so the eviction order was not displaced.
issues.legal_principle: Subsequent events may be considered cautiously to mould relief, with fairness to both sides, as stated in Pasupuleti Venkateswarlu v. Motor and General Traders. For a personal-requirement eviction claim to fail on account of later events, those events must wholly satisfy the landlord’s requirement, as stated in Hasmat Rai v. Raghunath Prasad. The Court also relied on Ramesh Kumar v. Kesho Ram and Kamleshwar Prasad v. Pradumanju Agarwal and distinguished the circumstances addressed in Ansuyaben Kantilal Bhatt v. Rashiklal Manilal Shah.

predicates.personal_need_eviction_case: A landlord brings an eviction proceeding on the ground that the premises are needed for the landlord or a family member.
predicates.bona_fide_need_found: The adjudicating authorities have found the landlord’s asserted personal or family need to be genuine.
predicates.subsequent_events_completely_satisfied_n: Later developments have wholly fulfilled or otherwise completely eclipsed the need for the premises.

issues.definition: In a personal-need eviction proceeding, later developments do not defeat a need found genuine unless those developments completely satisfy or eclipse it.
